title: Symmetry and how to break it

questions.heading: Identical Crews Make Every Plan Appear Once per Numbering of the Crews
questions.stem: A depot's model gives each delivery route a binary per truck, x[route, truck], for three identical trucks. One plan sends each truck on a different set of routes. How many 0/1 points of the model describe that plan?

options.text: 3, one for each truck that could take the first set
options.says: Choosing the first set's truck leaves two ways to place the second set: 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 numberings in all.

options.text: 8, one for each way to switch the 3 trucks on or off
options.says: Every truck is used in this plan; the copies come from renumbering the trucks, 3! = 6 ways.

options.text: 1, since a plan is the same whichever truck takes a set
options.says: To the business it is one plan; to the MILP each renumbering is a different x, as the 24 copies of the Ridge plan were.

options.text: 6, one for each way to number the 3 trucks in order
options.says: Right: 3! = 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 renumberings, each a different point with the same cost.

questions.heading: An Ordering Row Keeps at Least One Copy of Every Plan and Removes the Rest
questions.stem: A model of identical crews already orders them by load, L0 >= L1 >= L2. A colleague also adds the first-job rows, x[j, k] = 0 for every crew k after job j's position. What can this do?

options.text: Change the optimum, if no best plan's busiest crew holds job 0
options.says: Right: such a plan has no numbering that puts job 0's crew first and the busiest crew first; it loses every copy.

options.text: Nothing, since each family alone keeps a copy of every plan
options.says: Each keeps a copy, but each keeps a different numbering; a plan can lose its last copy when both are imposed.

options.text: Shrink the search for certain, since more copies of each plan are removed
options.says: Removing copies is not a promise of fewer nodes (load rows took more nodes than the plain model on 4 of 12 instances), and here it can remove whole plans.

options.text: Loosen the LP bound, since the model now carries more rows
options.says: Adding rows can only shrink the LP region; a bound never gets looser from an extra row.

questions.heading: Identical Jobs Are Symmetric Too: Count Them Instead of Naming Them
questions.stem: Twelve identical transformers each get a binary for each of 4 replacement years, 48 binaries, with a crew limit per year. Which model removes their symmetry and is also smaller?

options.text: The 48 binaries, plus rows that order the transformers in each year
options.says: Ordering rows break the symmetry but keep every binary and add rows; counting the transformers shrinks the model, as 57 variables became 25 for Ridge.

options.text: One binary per year, saying whether any transformer is replaced then
options.says: It drops how many are replaced, which the crew limit and the cost need; the count of identical items is what the model must keep.

options.text: One integer per year, 0 to 12, counting the transformers replaced then
options.says: Right: the transformers are identical, so only how many per year matters; 4 integers replace 48 binaries.

options.text: The 48 binaries, with the solver's symmetry detection switched on
options.says: Detection helps the search but leaves the model at 48 binaries; the counted model is smaller.
